column3: The Hebrew repeats the LORD’s name and says her mouth opened wide against her enemies; BSB uses “in whom” and “speaks boldly.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats the word for high or haughty speech.
The Hebrew has singular “bow” and active girding by those stumbling; BSB has plural “bows” and the passive “are equipped.”
The Hebrew names bread and says the hungry “ceased,” without a separate verb for hungering.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says the LORD makes poor and makes rich; BSB uses “sends poverty and wealth.”
The Hebrew describes inheriting a throne; BSB says He bestows it on them.
The Hebrew names feet rather than steps and describes the wicked being silenced rather than perishing.
The Hebrew has a singular object pronoun with the thundering; BSB has plural “them.”
The Hebrew says the boy was serving; BSB adds beginning to minister.
The Hebrew calls Eli’s sons “sons of worthlessness” and says they did not know the LORD; BSB has “wicked men” and “had no regard.”
The Hebrew begins an independent description of priestly custom; BSB attaches it to the previous negative with “or for.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly names the soul’s desire; BSB uses “whatever you want.”
The Hebrew explicitly names “the men” as despising the offering; BSB uses “they.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses “seed” and an asking or lending expression without explicitly saying “the one she dedicated.” It ends with singular “his place”; BSB has “home.”
The Hebrew says Samuel grew “with the LORD”; BSB has “in the presence of the LORD.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker and recipients unnamed in pronouns; BSB names Eli and his sons.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says he kept growing and was good with the LORD and people; BSB supplies “in stature” and the noun “favor.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew has an unnamed singular “him” for the chosen priest and speaks of going up on the altar; BSB supplies “your father” and “offer sacrifices.”
The Hebrew first addresses a plural “you” in kicking, then a singular “you” in honoring the sons; English BSB does not mark this distinction.
Close to the Hebrew.
